sub: 209 Joralemon Street, Brooklyn Community District 2, Council District 33
lead: If 250 Baltic shows how much can change without anyone voting on it, Borough Hall shows the opposite. Almost nothing here can change, and the reasons are three separate bodies of law answering to three different bodies of government. It is worth walking through because it maps the outer edge of what zoning can and cannot reach.

facts.d: Not R, C or M. The lot is mapped as public parkland.
Designated in its own right, not merely as part of a district.
So it carries both individual and district designation.
Held by the Department of Citywide Administrative Services.
Designed 1835 by Calvin Pollard, halted by the Panic of 1837, completed by Gamaliel King. Altered 1898.
It became Borough Hall when Brooklyn ceased to be its own city in 1898.

layers.t: The zoning is PARK, which is not really zoning at all
layers.b: PARK on a zoning map does not describe what may be built. It marks land mapped as a public park, which puts the Parks Department in charge rather than the Use Group tables. A public park is Use Group I, open uses, permitted as of right in every district in the city, so the park needs no permissive zoning to exist. The designation is not granting permission, it is recording a status.

layers.t: Changing it takes Albany, not City Hall
layers.b: Mapped parkland is held in the public trust. Converting it to any other use is called alienation, and it requires an act of the New York State Legislature signed by the Governor, normally with replacement parkland of equal or greater value. A City Council vote cannot do it. Neither can the City Planning Commission, the Board of Standards and Appeals, or the Mayor. This is a stronger protection than any zoning district provides, and it is the reason parkland is treated as effectively permanent.

layers.t: Landmark designation governs the building, twice over
layers.b: Borough Hall is an individual landmark and it also sits inside the Borough Hall Skyscraper Historic District. Individual designation is the stronger of the two: it attaches to this building specifically rather than to its contribution to a streetscape. Any exterior alteration needs Landmarks Preservation Commission approval before the Department of Buildings will issue a permit. But landmarking still has nothing to say about use. It governs what the building looks like, not what happens inside it.

Public ownership means that disposing of the site, leasing it, or changing what occupies it runs through city property rules and the budget process rather than through zoning. A private owner facing an unwanted rule can apply for a variance. The city cannot meaningfully apply to itself, so the question becomes a political and budgetary one instead of a land use one.

rows: 250 Baltic: R6 with a C1-3 overlay
Borough Hall: PARK, not an ordinary district
Not a zoning question at all
As of right under the R6
Albany, LPC and the city as owner

takeaway: Neither of these lots is a rezoning story, and that is the point. At 250 Baltic the rules already permit a great deal, so change happens without review. At Borough Hall the binding constraints are not zoning at all, so a rezoning would not unlock anything. In both cases the useful question is not whether to rezone, but which body of law is actually controlling.
